title: Judge Gives US Until Wednesday to Justify Holding Princeton Student Eva Yi Xie
excerpt: The government must show by 5 p.m. Wednesday why Xie's detention differs from other recent ICE cases, or she gets a bond hearing. Princeton students rallied Monday and Rep. Watson Coleman called the detention outrageous.
body:
• A federal judge has given the US government until 5 p.m. on Wednesday, November 25, 2026, to show why Princeton PhD student Eva Yi Xie's detention differs from other recent ICE detentions, and signalled he would grant a bond hearing if it cannot, PIX11 reported.
  • Hundreds of students and staff rallied at Princeton on Monday, November 23, under "Free Eva" and "Let Her Go" signs, and were urged to call their senators and representatives.
  • Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman called the detention "outrageous" in a statement and said her offices are following the case and pressing for Xie to return to Princeton.
  • Xie, detained at Reagan National Airport on November 19 after a neuroscience conference, remains held in Virginia; her lawyer says a pending asylum application allows her to live, work and study in the US while it is decided.

The case of Eva Yi Xie, the Princeton neuroscience PhD student detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) last week, now has a deadline. According to PIX11, a federal judge has given the government until 5 p.m. on Wednesday to show why Xie's case differs from other recent detentions of non-citizens by ICE, and signalled that if it cannot justify her continued detention, he would grant her a bond hearing and release.

Xie was taken into custody on Thursday, November 19, at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport as she returned from the Society for Neuroscience conference, where she had presented her research. A judge has already barred ICE from removing her from Virginia while her habeas corpus petition is heard.

Princeton rallies

On Monday evening, students and staff rallied on Princeton's campus behind signs reading "Free Eva," "Let Her Go" and "Bring Eva Home," News 12 New Jersey and CBS News Philadelphia reported. Organisers handed attendees the phone numbers of lawmakers and asked them to call their home-state senators and representatives and write letters pressing for her release; participants were also given LED candles to place in windows. Assistant Professor Benjamin Eysenbach, one of Xie's teachers, questioned how this could happen to his student.

Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman, whose district includes Princeton, issued a statement calling the detention "outrageous" and a reflection of what she described as the "foolishness and cruelty" of the Trump administration's immigration policy. She said her offices are following the case, that she is in contact with congressional colleagues, and that she wants Xie returned to Princeton to resume her studies. Xie's adviser, Professor Carlos Brody, and her colleagues have also been working with Senator Andy Kim on her case.

The two accounts of her status

Xie, a Chinese-born third-year doctoral student who has lived in the United States since 2016, is being held at a detention facility in Virginia. Her attorney, Kerry Doyle, argues that Xie has permission to live, work and study in the country while her asylum application is pending, and that she has no criminal background. The Department of Homeland Security says Xie was admitted temporarily in 2016, overstayed, and has never held valid authorisation to study in the United States, and that a pending asylum application does not confer legal status.

What happens next

Wednesday's 5 p.m. deadline is the next decision point: if the government's filing does not satisfy the judge, Xie could get a bond hearing and release while her habeas petition and asylum case proceed. Princeton has arranged legal counsel for her, and Graduate School Dean Rodney D. Priestley has said the university is distressed by the arrest and remains in contact with her family and legal team. For international students watching the case, the practical position is unchanged: a pending asylum application is the basis of her legal team's argument, and the court, not ICE, will decide whether she waits for its outcome in detention or at home.
